name: Aisha Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential. Could you start by telling me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I'm on a modular housing crew. The houses are built in a factory in big boxes, kitchens and bathrooms already fitted, then trucked to the site, and a crane drops them onto the foundations. My job is bolting the boxes together, sealing the joins, finishing the floors and walls where two boxes meet, and fixing whatever got knocked about on the motorway. We can set a whole house in a day, which still amazes me. Then on Saturdays, Luka and I run a little business building decks and garden pergolas, and that's my baby.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy speed and I enjoy being my own boss on Saturdays. I use AI for everything on the business side: it turns a customer's photo of their garden into a picture of the deck they could have, it writes the quote, it plans the cut list so we waste less timber. What wears me out is having two jobs and two kids, Mia's fourteen and Jonah's eleven, and church on Sunday, and somehow also cooking dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's still a great tool, just not the end of the world. I'd post something on the business page like, AI drew your deck, Aisha built it. I like that line, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be fine for me. I already get a lot from it, the quotes and the designs save me hours every week. If it stops there, my weekday job stays the same and my Saturday business keeps growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as I am. Keep using the AI for the business, keep saving, and maybe take on a second Saturday helper so Luka can have a weekend off now and then. We've been talking about buying a bigger trailer for the timber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using AI so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mia showed me, two years ago, for a school project, and I thought, I could use that for quotes. Now I can do a quote in ten minutes on my phone in the customer's garden, and they sign it while I'm standing there. Luka still does his garage invoices by hand, it drives me mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the chance to grow. I had ideas about bigger tools, machines that cut the timber for you from the design. But honestly, I'd be fine without that. I like a world that's steady.

S0.say: I'd say it's still a great tool, just not the end of the world, and post on the business page that AI drew your deck and Aisha built it.
S0.think: Privately it'd be fine, since AI already saves her hours each week on quotes and designs. Her weekday job would stay the same and her Saturday business would keep growing.
S0.do: Keeps going as she is, using AI for the deck business and saving. Considers hiring a second Saturday helper and buying a bigger trailer for timber.
S0.quote: Now I can do a quote in ten minutes on my phone in the customer's garden, and they sign it while I'm standing there.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha is energetic and entrepreneurial, and her Saturday deck business is clearly where her heart is. Her AI use is practical and daily, learned from her teenage daughter. She is content with the plateau and would simply keep building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. Small businesses can do what the big ones do now, for a fraction of the cost. I'd say get on with it, don't wait for someone to hand you a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. Modular building is half factory already, so more machines in the factory doesn't scare me, someone still bolts the boxes together on site. And for the Saturday business, it's a chance to grow, because I can do things now that used to need an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a small cutting machine that reads the AI design and cuts the timber, they're maybe eight or nine thousand, from savings. I'd take on a helper for Saturdays and maybe Fridays too. And I'd learn every new tool at the modular job as soon as it came in, because I like being the one who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Luka think about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks I'm a bit mad, but he trusts me with the money. He's careful, I'm quick, and that works for us. He'd make me sit down with the numbers before I bought anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guys at the modular job who don't want to learn anything. There's one, Rick, who's been there longer than me and refuses to use the tablet. I'd help him if he asked, but I won't drag him.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance for people willing to work and learn, since small businesses can now do what big ones do at a fraction of the cost. Get on with it rather than wait for someone to hand you a plan.
S1.think: Privately she thinks it's good for her, since modular building is already half factory work and someone still joins the boxes on site. For her Saturday business it's a chance to grow without needing an office.
S1.do: Buys a cutting machine that cuts timber from AI designs for about eight or nine thousand from savings and hires a helper for Saturdays and maybe Fridays. Learns each new tool at her weekday job as soon as it arrives.
S1.quote: He's careful, I'm quick, and that works for us.
S1.fieldNote: Aisha's traditional, free-market outlook shows in her focus on small business and self-reliance. She moves first with real money and enjoys being the one who knows the tools. Her husband acts as the careful check on her speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small businesses need room to compete, so don't let the big firms buy up all the robots and crush everyone. Keep the rules simple, cut the red tape. I'd say it on the business page and at church to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one worries me. I'm quick, but two years isn't long enough for a little deck business to compete with a big company that buys a hundred robots on day one. And my weekday job would go, because a robot can bolt boxes together, so it's just me, Luka's garage and our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Day one, I'd look at buying a robot or the best machine I could afford for the deck business, maybe twenty or thirty thousand from our savings, because owning one is better than being replaced by one. I'd keep a year of cash in the bank, no matter what. And I'd cut the extras, no new car, no holiday, until I saw how it went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. In control of what I can control, worried about what I can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mia and Jonah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're a family that works, and we'll find a way. Mia would probably have ideas, she's the one who showed me AI in the first place. Jonah would want to know if the robot could build him a treehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said owning a robot is better than being replaced by one. But you also said a big company could crush a small business. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't, fully. I'd be betting on customers who want a local family business, someone they know, someone who'll come back if something's wrong. Maybe that's not enough, but it's the bet I'd make.

S2.say: I'd say small businesses need room to compete, so big firms shouldn't be allowed to buy all the robots and crush everyone, and red tape should be cut. I'd say it on the business page and at church.
S2.think: Privately she worries that two years isn't enough for a small deck business to compete with big firms buying robots on day one. Her weekday job would go, leaving her husband's garage, the business and their savings.
S2.do: Buys a robot or the best machine she can afford for the deck business, around twenty or thirty thousand from savings, while keeping a year of cash in the bank. Cuts extras like a new car and holiday until she sees how things go.
S2.feel: Anxious: in control of what she can control, worried about what she can't.
S2.quote: I'd be betting on customers who want a local family business, someone they know, someone who'll come back if something's wrong.
S2.fieldNote: Aisha's fear is not technology but scale: big firms buying robots faster than small ones can. She admitted she can't fully square her plan with that risk, and that she's betting on loyalty to local family businesses. Her anxiety is real but she stays active.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for small businesses to get ready, if the government stays out of the way and lets people build. Get the tools, get the customers, get going. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a different story for me. I can build the deck business into something real, with machines and maybe two or three staff, before AGI fully hits. By the time the weekday job goes, I'd want the business to be paying the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd buy the cutting machine and hire a Friday and Saturday helper. Year two, I'd go part-time at the modular job and grow the business to three or four days a week. By year three or four, I'd leave the modular job and run the business full-time, with whatever robots make sense by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lots. Big firms could undercut me, timber could get expensive, I could get it wrong. But I've got savings to fall back on and Luka's garage, so even if it fails, we eat. And I'd rather fail trying than sit in the cabin waiting for the bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your faith come into all this, if at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It keeps me steady. I pray about the big decisions, and I talk to our pastor, who ran a shop for twenty years before he was a pastor. He's the one who told me, work hard, be honest, and trust that the rest isn't all on you.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for small businesses to get ready if government stays out of the way: get the tools, get the customers, get going.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years lets her build the deck business into something real, with machines and a few staff, before AGI fully arrives. She wants the business paying the bills by the time her weekday job goes.
S3.do: Buys the cutting machine and hires a helper in year one, goes part-time at the modular job and grows the business in year two, and leaves to run it full-time by year three or four with whatever robots make sense.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.
S3.quote: I'd rather fail trying than sit in the cabin waiting for the bad news.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Aisha lays out a clear staged move from employee to business owner. Her faith, and her pastor's own small-business past, give her steadiness. She has a realistic view of the risks but a cushion that makes failure survivable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for anyone willing to work. Learn, build, look after your family. I'd say it with a smile, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is great for me. I'd grow the business slowly, keep the weekday job for steady money for a while, and by fifty-three I'd hope to have a proper family business, maybe with Mia involved if she wants. AGI would be something I'd use rather than something that happened to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the modular job for four or five years and grow the deck business on the side. I'd add machines as they got cheaper and better, and keep investing a bit each month in the business and in savings. And I'd talk to Mia and Jonah about whether they'd want to be part of it, without pushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited about it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a family business look like for you, ten years out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A yard with our name on the gate, a couple of machines, a van or two, and people who trust us. Maybe Luka's garage next door. Something we built that the kids could take over if they wanted, and if they don't, they'll have learned what work looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rick, from the modular job, still, and men like him. Ten years is plenty of warning, but not everyone takes the warning. I'd want churches and families to step up for them, and maybe I'd hire one or two, if they wanted to learn.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for anyone willing to work: learn, build and look after your family. I'd say it with a smile, honestly.
S4.think: Privately ten years is great for her, with time to grow the business slowly while keeping steady weekday pay. By fifty-three she hopes to have a proper family business and to use AGI rather than have it happen to her.
S4.do: Keeps the modular job for four or five years while growing the deck business, adding machines as they get cheaper and investing monthly in the business and savings. Talks with her children about joining the business without pushing them.
S4.quote: A yard with our name on the gate, a couple of machines, a van or two, and people who trust us.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Aisha is fully confident, seeing AGI as a tool for building a family business. Her concern for workers who don't heed warnings is genuine, and she'd look to churches, families and her own hiring rather than the state. Her vision of a yard with the family name on the gate is vivid and specific.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time for a small business to get going before the big firms take everything. What would help is rules that stop a few giant companies owning all the robots, cheap loans for small businesses to buy machines, and less paperwork so people can just start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about trust. People still pick who builds their deck by who they know at church or the school gate. I don't know if that survives robots, but I'm betting a lot on it.

headlineQuote: People still pick who builds their deck by who they know at church or the school gate.
portrait: Aisha is a 43-year-old modular housing installer who also runs a Saturday deck and pergola business with her mechanic husband, and she uses AI every day for designs and quotes. She believes in small business, hard work, family and faith, and wants government to cut red tape and stop big firms monopolising robots. She is calm and even excited through the plateau and steady pictures, anxious in fast AGI because big companies could outpace small ones, and steadily more confident with five and ten years as she plans to turn the deck business into a full-time family firm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because a small business would have no time to get going before big firms took everything.
whatWouldHelp: Rules stopping a few giant companies owning all the robots, cheap loans for small businesses to buy machines, and less paperwork so people can start.
